title: Temple Stay in Korea: How to Book, What It Costs, and What to Expect
html:
Spend one night inside a real, working Buddhist temple — wake up before sunrise to a hand bell, eat a silent meal from a wooden bowl, and try bowing 108 times. That's a temple stay (templestay), one of Korea's most unique overnight experiences, and you don't need to be Buddhist, or even religious at all, to try it. Here's how it actually works, what it costs, and what to expect if you book one.

What Exactly Is a Temple Stay?

Jogyesa Temple in Seoul, the head temple of Korea's Jogye Order and a common starting point for first-timers curious about temple stay.

A temple stay is an official program, mostly run by temples belonging to the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism, where any visitor — Korean or foreign, Buddhist or not — can stay overnight inside a working temple and follow a simplified version of a monk's daily routine. It's not a sermon or a sales pitch for religion; most people (including plenty of Koreans) do it purely for the quiet, the forest setting, and the novelty of unplugging for a day. Think of it less like a religious retreat and more like a very calm, very early-rising homestay.

Two Kinds of Programs — and What They Cost

Most temples that run templestay offer two different styles of program, at different price points.

  • Experience Program: A structured schedule — dawn chanting, 108 bows, a formal temple meal, meditation, and usually a craft activity like making a lotus lantern or prayer beads. This is the one most first-time visitors pick. Typical cost: roughly 70,000–100,000 KRW per person for one night, two days.
  • Relaxation (Rest) Program: Much less structured — you join only the basic temple meals and services, and otherwise spend the time walking the grounds, reading, or resting. Typical cost: roughly 50,000–80,000 KRW.
  • Day Program (no overnight): A shorter, few-hours visit with a temple tour, tea time, and a short talk with a monk — a good option if your schedule is tight. Typical cost: roughly 20,000–30,000 KRW.

Prices vary by temple and season, and a few central Seoul temples with premium programs can run 150,000–220,000 KRW. Korea's Buddhist Cultural Foundation also occasionally runs limited-time discount campaigns just for foreign visitors (one ran through September 2026 at a flat 30,000 KRW) — these come and go, so always check the current price on the official site before you plan around one.

How and Where to Book

Woljeongsa Temple in Pyeongchang, Gangwon-do — one of many temples offering templestay with English program information.

The official booking site is templestay.com, run by the Jogye Order's Cultural Corps for Buddhist Studies, with a full English version. You can search by region, date, and program type, and see which temples currently have English-speaking staff or English materials. For most popular temples, especially on weekends or during cherry blossom (spring) and foliage (autumn) season, book 2–4 weeks ahead — walk-ins are rarely accepted.

If you'd rather ask questions in person first, the Templestay Information Center near Insadong in Seoul (just by Jogyesa) has English-speaking staff who can help you pick a program and book, even if you're not fully sure what you want yet. A few temples that are especially well set up for foreign visitors: Woljeongsa (a forest-walk temple in Gangwon-do), and Golgulsa in Gyeongju, known for combining temple stay with a traditional monk martial art called Seonmudo.

What a Typical Day Looks Like

Most one-night programs follow a similar daily rhythm, whichever temple you choose.

You'll usually check in during the afternoon, change into a simple vest or robe the temple lends you (worn over your own clothes), and get a short tour. Dinner is a formal temple meal called barugongyang, eaten in near-silence from wooden bowls — the custom is to finish everything on your plate, down to the last grain of rice, as a way of not wasting food. After dinner there's an evening chanting service, then usually free time or tea with a monk, with lights out around 9–10 PM.

The next morning starts early — often around 3–4 AM, woken by a monk striking a wooden hand bell (moktak) and a temple bell. This is followed by dawn chanting and, in the Experience Program, 108 bows. Breakfast comes after, followed by a craft activity or free time before checkout, usually by late morning.

What to Bring, Wear, and Keep in Mind

Comfortable walking shoes help — you'll cross this kind of forest path at some temples, and you'll be sitting on the floor and taking shoes on and off a lot.

  • Clothing: Wear loose, comfortable, modest clothing — no shorts or sleeveless tops. The temple provides a simple vest to wear over it, but your own clothes still need to cover shoulders and knees.
  • Shoes: You'll remove your shoes constantly (every indoor space), so slip-on shoes are much easier than lace-ups.
  • Food: All temple meals are vegetarian and skip the "five pungent" ingredients (garlic, onion, chives, leek, and a wild chive relative) by Buddhist tradition — worth knowing if you're a picky eater, since there's usually no substitute menu.
  • Phone use: Most programs ask you to keep your phone off or silent during ceremonies and meals, and some ask you to hand it in overnight. Treat it as part of the experience, not a restriction.
  • No special knowledge needed: You don't need to know how to bow, chant, or meditate beforehand — monks and staff walk you through everything step by step.

One local-perspective note: plenty of Koreans book a temple stay for exactly the same reason some travelers do — not for religious reasons, but as a cheap, screen-free weekend reset from city life. If "digital detox" or "quiet overnight in nature" sounds appealing, that's reason enough to try one.

Program Type Structure Typical Duration Typical Cost Best For
Experience Program Structured (chanting, 108 bows, craft activity) 1 night, 2 days 70,000–100,000 KRW First-timers wanting the full cultural experience
Relaxation (Rest) Program Mostly free time, basic services only 1 night, 2 days 50,000–80,000 KRW Travelers who just want a quiet break
Day Program Short visit, tea + talk with a monk A few hours, no overnight 20,000–30,000 KRW Tight schedules or a quick introduction

💬 Thinking about trying a temple stay, or not sure which program fits your trip? Drop your question in the comments below — happy to help!
meta_description: A beginner's guide to Korea's temple stay: program types, typical costs, how to book, and what a day really looks like.
